first_impression.reaction: Good start. It says straight away that I'm probably not covered the way I assume, and it says the sources are public Australian ones and that this isn't financial advice. Nobody is selling me a policy in the first three paragraphs, so I'll keep going. First thing I did was skip to the FAQ and the 'what to check' table, and they hold up.

journey.quote: This guide follows the ring from the counter to a proposal abroad and on to the wedding, using only public Australian sources.
journey.reaction: Sources named up front. That's what I want. I'll check a couple of them against Moneysmart, but at least they're telling me where it comes from.

journey.section: What the PDS is, and why it matters
journey.quote: Every point below is a question to put to your insurer, not a statement of what any particular policy does.
journey.reaction: Honest about its limits. No one is pretending to know what my policy says. Good.

journey.quote: Most contents policies set a maximum you can claim for certain items, and you pay the difference above that limit.
journey.reaction: That's the catch, and they actually say it. What I'd like next is a rough idea of what those limits usually are, even a range, but I get that it varies by policy.

journey.section: What to check in any policy
journey.quote: | Is loss covered, as well as theft and damage? | PDS, list of insured events |
journey.reaction: This table is the most useful thing on the page. I'd copy it straight into my spreadsheet and run three quotes through it.

journey.quote: A stone that falls out of its setting is the case couples ask about most, and whether it counts as loss or damage depends on the wording, so check your policy and ask your insurer how they treat it.
journey.reaction: 'The case couples ask about most' according to who? Everything else has a source and this one doesn't. Small, but it's exactly the sort of line I'd notice.

journey.quote: In Australia, a valuer does not have to belong to a professional body.
journey.reaction: Didn't know that, and it's useful. Tells me to check who's doing the valuation instead of trusting the jeweller's piece of paper.

journey.quote: The ring box is the hardest object to hide and the easiest to leave behind on a sun lounger.
journey.reaction: Filler. Doesn't hurt much, but it's colour, not information.

journey.section: Carry-on, travel dates and hotel safes
journey.quote: Smartraveller lists what standard travel policies typically do not cover: items left unattended, items not stored in a hotel safe when one was available, items left with someone met on the trip, and items stolen from checked baggage or a locked car.
journey.reaction: Specific, sourced exclusions. This is the bit that actually changes what I'd do on the trip.

journey.section: Carry-on, travel dates and hotel safes
journey.quote: A Wedded Advisor plans venue, travel, vendors and payments, anywhere in the world, as your single point of contact, so the logistics around the rings sit inside one plan.
journey.reaction: Here's the pitch. It comes after the evidence at least, and it's short. But a planner doesn't insure my ring, so linking the two feels like a stretch. And my first question is still: what does the Advisor cost and do they take a cut from venues?

journey.quote: AFCA may not be able to help if a court has decided the matter, if the complaint falls outside its rules or time limits, or if the firm is not a member, so check AFCA's site early.
journey.reaction: They even tell me when the escape hatch doesn't work. That's the kind of trade-off most articles leave out.

journey.quote: when you are ready, a Wedded Advisor will plan the venue and the travel with you from first idea to the last dance, working in your time zone and quoting in AUD.
journey.reaction: 'From first idea to the last dance' is the only properly fluffy line in the piece. 'Quoting in AUD' is concrete and I like that. Still doesn't tell me the fee model.

unanswered_questions: What are typical per-item limits on Australian contents policies for jewellery, even as a rough range?
Roughly what does it cost per year to specify a ring of a given value? Is this a percentage-of-value thing?
Who says a lost stone is the case couples ask about most?
How is a Wedded Advisor paid, and do they take commission from venues or suppliers?
Does Wedded Wonderland get anything from insurers or jewellers linked or mentioned here?

turn_offs_found.quote: A stone that falls out of its setting is the case couples ask about most
turn_offs_found.why: Unsupported claim in an article where everything else is sourced. Stands out for the wrong reason.

turn_offs_found.quote: a Wedded Advisor will plan the venue and the travel with you from first idea to the last dance
turn_offs_found.why: Emotional sign-off language. Minor, but it's the one place the tone slips from facts to marketing.

would_share_with: My fiancee, as the checklist to go through with our insurer
A mate who's about to buy a ring

cta_reaction.quote: See [how a Wedded Advisor plans the wedding travel](/wonderland-concierge).
cta_reaction.why: It comes after the evidence, not before, so it doesn't annoy me. I'd click only to look for the fee model. If that page doesn't say how the Advisor is paid, I'm out.

top_3_changes: Source or cut 'A stone that falls out of its setting is the case couples ask about most'. Rephrase as 'A common worry is a stone falling out of its setting' if there's no source.
Replace 'from first idea to the last dance' with something concrete about what the Advisor actually does.
If a public source gives typical jewellery per-item limits or premium ranges, add one sourced figure; numbers would move this from good to bookmark-worthy.
